t.2.27.1: But Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, being consoled by Rāma, spoke these words to her husband for the sake of dwelling in the forest.
t.2.27.2: Sītā, deeply agitated, out of love and out of wounded pride, reproached broad-chested Rāghava.
t.2.27.3: O Rāma, what did my father, the Vaideha, lord of Mithilā, think of you when he obtained you as his son-in-law, a woman in the form of a man?
t.2.27.5: Having done what, then, are you so dejected, or from what quarter does fear come to you, that you wish to abandon me, who have no refuge but you?
t.2.27.6: O hero, know me to be like Sāvitrī, who was devoted to Satyavat, the son of Dyumatsena; know me as one who abides under your control alone.
t.2.27.4: For this world of men, out of ignorance, will speak a falsehood when it says that in Rāma there is no supreme splendour such as there is in the blazing sun.
t.2.27.7: But apart from you, O sinless one, I will never look upon another man, not even in my mind. I would go with you, Rāghava, and not be like some other woman who brings disgrace upon her family.
t.2.27.8: Yet you yourself, O Rāma, like an actor who trades on his wife, wish to hand me over to others: me, your chaste wife, wedded to you as a maiden and long dwelling with you.
t.2.27.9: Therefore you ought not to set out for the forest without taking me along. Whether it be austerity, or the wilderness, or heaven itself, let it be together with you.
t.2.27.11: The kuśa and kāśa grasses, the reeds and rushes, and the thorny trees on the path will feel to me as soft to the touch as cotton or deerskin while I walk with you.
t.2.27.10: Walking behind you, I shall feel no weariness at all on the path there, no more than I would on couches of pleasure.
t.2.27.12: The dust stirred up by mighty winds that will settle upon me, O beloved, I shall regard as the most precious sandalwood.
t.2.27.14: Whatever leaf, root or fruit you yourself gather and give me, whether little or much, that will be to me like the taste of nectar.
t.2.27.13: When I, a wanderer of the woods, shall sit upon the grassy meadows at the forest's edge, what could be more delightful than that, even on couches spread with fine woollen coverlets?
t.2.27.15: There I shall not remember my mother, nor my father, nor my home, as I enjoy the flowers and fruits of each season.
t.2.27.16: And having gone there, you shall not see anything unpleasant; nor shall there be grief for you on my account, nor shall I be hard to support.
t.2.27.18: If you will not take me, calm and eager as I am, to the forest, I shall drink poison this very day, so that I may not fall into the power of my enemies.
t.2.27.17: Whatever is with you is heaven, and whatever is without you is hell. Knowing this, O Rāma, attain the highest joy together with me.
t.2.27.19: For even afterwards, through grief, there would be no life at all for me, abandoned by you, O lord; better, then, is death at that very moment.
t.2.27.21: Thus she, burning with grief, having lamented much and piteously, cried out aloud in her distress, tightly embracing her husband.
t.2.27.20: For I cannot bear this grief even for a moment; how much less, in my sorrow, for ten years and three and one more?
t.2.27.23: From her eyes flowed water clear as crystal, born of her anguish, like water trickling from a pair of lotuses.
t.2.27.22: Pierced by his many words as a she-elephant is pierced by poisoned arrows, she let loose the tears she had long held back, as the fire-stick releases fire.
t.2.27.24: Embracing her with both arms as she lay grief-stricken, as though senseless, Rāma then spoke these words, reassuring her.
t.2.27.25: O queen, I would not desire even heaven at the cost of your sorrow. For, like Svayambhū, I have no fear of anything from any quarter.
t.2.27.26: O fair-faced one, without knowing your whole intention, I did not favor your dwelling in the forest, though I am able to protect you.
t.2.27.27: Since you were created to dwell in the forest together with me, O Maithilī, you cannot be abandoned by me, just as fame cannot be abandoned by a self-possessed man.
t.2.27.28: But, O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk, this is the dharma practised by the virtuous of old, and today I follow it just as Suvarcalā follows the sun.
t.2.27.29: This indeed is dharma, O lovely-hipped one: obedience to one's father and mother. And therefore, having transgressed their command, I could not bear to live.
t.2.27.31: Give jewels to the brāhmaṇas and food to the mendicants and to those who ask for it; make haste, do not delay.
t.2.27.30: Just as my father, standing firm on the path of truth and dharma, commands me, so do I wish to act, for that is the eternal dharma. Follow me, timid one, and be my companion in dharma.
t.2.27.32: Knowing that her own going was agreeable to her husband, the queen, overjoyed, quickly set about giving away her possessions.
t.2.27.33: Then the illustrious and high-minded lady, overjoyed and with her heart fulfilled, having heeded her husband's words, began to give away wealth and jewels to those who uphold dharma.
